name: Dutch Defense: Leningrad Variation
summary: The Leningrad Dutch fuses ...f5 with a King's-Indian-style fianchetto, aiming for the ...e5 break and sharp kingside play.
intro: The Leningrad Variation is the most dynamic branch of the Dutch Defence, reached after moves such as 1.d4 f5 2.g3 Nf6 3.Bg2 g6 4.Nf3 Bg7 5.O-O O-O 6.c4 d6. Black couples the trademark Dutch pawn on f5 with a kingside fianchetto, producing a structure closely related to the King's Indian Defence. The play is fighting and double-edged, with Black staking everything on active piece play and central breaks rather than solid restraint.
line: d4 f5 g3 Nf6 Bg2 g6 Nf3 Bg7 O-O O-O c4 d6

sections.heading: Strategic ideas
paragraphs: The Leningrad set-up marries two ideas: the Dutch advance ...f5, which stakes a claim to the e4-square and prepares kingside expansion, and the King's Indian fianchetto with ...g6 and ...Bg7, which puts the dark-squared bishop on its most active diagonal. The resulting pawn skeleton, with pawns on d6 and f5, is geared toward the central break ...e5, after which Black hopes to seize the initiative in the centre and on the kingside. Because both sides fianchetto and castle short, the middlegame often revolves around competing pawn breaks: Black's ...e5 (and sometimes ...g5-g4) against White's space-gaining advances on the queenside.

White's trumps are space and structure. By meeting ...f5 with the calm fianchetto and c4, White gains room to expand with d5 and queenside operations, and the advance d4-d5 can blunt the g7-bishop and pose questions about Black's central intentions. Black must be alert to the drawbacks of the ...f5 structure: the e6-square and the a2-g8 diagonal can be sensitive, and an ill-timed ...e5 may leave weaknesses. The typical struggle sees Black manoeuvring the queen to e8 and then to the kingside, preparing ...e5 or ...f4 to open lines, while White exploits the queenside majority and the central tension to generate counterplay of his own.

sections.heading: Main variations
paragraphs: The most characteristic plan for Black is the queen manoeuvre ...Qe8, clearing the way for ...e5 and eyeing the kingside via ...Qh5 or ...Qg6. After the central break, positions can open sharply, and Black's attacking chances hinge on the mobility of the g7-bishop and the f- and e-pawns. White most often replies with the natural d5 and Nc3, staking out queenside space and inviting Black to declare whether the counterplay will come with ...e5, ...c6 to challenge the d5-pawn, or ...Na6-c5 to pressure White's centre.

White has more than one route to an edge. A common approach is Nc3 and d5 followed by expansion with b4 and play on the c-file, restraining ...e5 and probing the queenside. Alternatives include quieter set-ups that keep the tension and rely on the safer structure, as well as ideas with an early b3 and Bb2 to contest the long diagonal. For Black, the choice between an immediate ...e5, a preparatory ...Nc6 or ...c6, and the sharp ...g5-g4 pawn storm defines the flavour of the game, but in every case the thematic ...e5 break remains the strategic focal point of the Leningrad.

sections.heading: History and background
paragraphs: The Leningrad Variation is named after the Soviet city where it was developed and refined in the mid-twentieth century, and it represents the most ambitious modern interpretation of the old Dutch Defence. Whereas classical Dutch set-ups such as the Stonewall emphasise restraint and a fixed pawn chain, the Leningrad borrows the fighting spirit of the King's Indian, aiming for active piece play and central counterattack. It became a favourite of players seeking unbalanced, winning chances with Black against 1.d4 and has been employed by a number of strong grandmasters. Today it retains a solid reputation as a combative, theory-rich system for those who relish sharp, double-edged struggles.

keyIdeas: Black combines the Dutch ...f5 with a King's-Indian ...g6 and ...Bg7 fianchetto.
The central ...e5 break is Black's principal strategic goal.
The g7-bishop and the f-pawn drive Black's kingside ambitions.
White uses space and the d4-d5 advance to restrain and probe the queenside.
The ...Qe8-h5/g6 manoeuvre redeploys the queen toward the kingside.
Black accepts a slightly loose structure in return for dynamic activity.
